title: Making a case for college: A genre-based college admission essay intervention for underserved high school students
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether explicit genre-based instruction can improve underserved high school seniors’ college admission essay writing and their self-efficacy for writing in that genre. The authors frame college admission essays as a high-stakes, gate-keeping form of writing that many low-income and ethnically diverse students are expected to produce for college access, yet often do not receive direct instruction on in regular secondary English classes. The study asks whether teaching the specific features of college admission essays helps students write better essays and feel more confident writing them.

The intervention was a six-week features-based writing workshop built around explicit teaching of genre elements in college admission essays. Students in the treatment condition received 10 instructional sessions including skill lessons, models/examples, practice, sharing, peer or instructor feedback, and revision. The curriculum taught features such as selecting a strong topic, audience awareness, introductions, dialogue, description, explaining significance (the “so what?”), connecting to outside texts or events, and writing conclusions. The comparison group completed the same pre/post essay and self-efficacy measures but otherwise received business-as-usual English instruction from their regular teacher, described as mostly literary analysis and not college admission essay instruction.

Participants were 41 12th-grade students at one urban public high school in the southwestern United States, primarily low-income and multi-ethnic, with many first-generation college-bound students and many previously classified as English Language Learners. Two intact classrooms were assigned by coin toss to treatment or comparison conditions. The intervention was delivered by a doctoral student in English Education, with assistance from the regular classroom teacher. Outcomes included rubric-scored pre/post college admission essays and a self-efficacy survey specific to college admission essay writing.

The study found that students who received the genre-based intervention scored significantly higher on posttest essay quality than the comparison group after controlling for pretest scores, and they also showed significantly greater gains in writing self-efficacy. The authors conclude that explicit, features-based instruction in authentic high-stakes writing genres may be a promising way to support underserved high school students’ writing development and college access. They also argue that college admission essay instruction should be incorporated into secondary writing curricula, especially in schools serving low-income and ethnically diverse students.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental group comparison study in K-12 with pre/post measures, a comparison condition, and reported statistical tests, but it is not a randomized controlled trial at the student level and has notable limitations including small sample size, convenience sampling, and some analytic assumption violations.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are substantial, with between-group variance explained of R²=0.46 for essay quality and R²=0.42 for self-efficacy, indicating a medium-to-large impact in a priority population of low-income, multi-ethnic high school students.

finding.finding_summary: This quasi-experimental study examined a non-technology, features-based genre-writing intervention for 12th-grade college admission essays. Students in the treatment group outperformed the comparison group receiving business-as-usual English instruction on posttest essay quality after controlling for pretest, F(1,38)=29.74, p<0.05, with R²=0.46; adjusted posttest means were 4.91 (SD=0.71, n=17) for treatment versus 3.68 (SD=0.78, n=22) for comparison on a 6-point holistic rubric.
finding.measure: Holistic rubric-based quality of college admission essays (6-point writing rubric assessing ideas/content, organization, voice, word choice, sentence fluency, conventions)
finding.study_size: n=41 overall; analytic table reports treatment n=17 and comparison n=22 for essay outcome
finding.std_deviation: Treatment posttest SD=0.71; comparison posttest SD=0.78; treatment pretest SD=0.60; comparison pretest SD=0.90

finding.finding_summary: The genre-based writing intervention also increased students’ writing self-efficacy relative to business-as-usual instruction. On self-efficacy difference scores, treatment and comparison groups differed significantly, F(1,36)=48.50, p<0.01, with R²=0.42; mean self-efficacy rose from 5.91 to 8.06 in the treatment group and declined slightly from 5.85 to 5.69 in the comparison group.
finding.measure: Self-reported college-admission-essay writing self-efficacy using a 15-item Likert-type confidence scale
finding.study_size: n=41 overall; analytic table reports treatment n=16 and comparison n=21 for self-efficacy outcome
finding.std_deviation: Treatment posttest SD=1.05; comparison posttest SD=1.71; treatment pretest SD=1.88; comparison pretest SD=1.79
